title: Count Triplets with Even XOR Set Bits II
statement:
Three integer arrays `a`, `b` and `c` are given. Choose an index `i` of `a`, an index `j` of `b` and an index `k` of `c`, and look at the bitwise XOR `a[i] ^ b[j] ^ c[k]`. Count the choices `(i, j, k)` for which this XOR has an **even** number of `1` bits in its binary form, and return the count.

Choices are distinguished by their indices, so equal values at different positions are counted separately. A XOR equal to `0` has zero `1` bits, and zero is even.
signature: long tripletCount(int[] a, int[] b, int[] c)
notes:
## Intuition

Trying every triplet costs O(|a|·|b|·|c|), up to 10^15 steps. The way out is that XOR never changes the parity of the total number of `1` bits: `x ^ y` keeps every bit where exactly one of `x` and `y` has a `1`, so it has `ones(x) + ones(y) - 2·ones(x & y)` ones, which has the same parity as `ones(x) + ones(y)`. Applied twice, `a[i] ^ b[j] ^ c[k]` has an even number of ones exactly when the three set-bit parities of `a[i]`, `b[j]` and `c[k]` add up to an even number. So every number only matters through its parity, and counting how many numbers of each array have an even or an odd number of ones is enough.

## Approach

1. `countParities(values)` returns `counts`, where `counts[p]` is how many values have set-bit parity `p`. For each value it clears the lowest `1` bit (`rest &= rest - 1`) until nothing is left, flipping `parity` once per cleared bit.
2. Compute `countA`, `countB` and `countC`.
3. For every parity `parityA` of the element from `a` and `parityB` of the element from `b`, the element from `c` must have parity `parityA ^ parityB` so that the three add up to an even number. Add the product of the three counts to `total`.
4. Return `total`.

## Example 1, step by step

`a = [1]`: one `1` bit, so `countA = [0, 1]`. `b = [2]` (binary `10`) gives `countB = [0, 1]`, and `c = [3]` (binary `11`) gives `countC = [1, 0]`. The four parity pairs give `0·0·1`, `0·1·0`, `1·0·0` and, for `parityA = 1`, `parityB = 1`, `1·1·countC[0] = 1`. So `total = 1`; indeed `1 ^ 2 ^ 3 = 0`, which has zero ones.

## Complexity

- Time: O((|a| + |b| + |c|) · 30): each value needs one loop step per `1` bit, at most 30 for values up to 10^9.
- Space: O(1): two counters per array.

## Pitfalls

- The answer can reach 10^15, beyond a 32-bit `int`: Java needs `long` and C `long long` for the products.
- A XOR of `0` has zero ones, which is even, so such triplets count.
- Equal values at different indices are different triplets; do not deduplicate.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `countParities` | helper that counts one array's values by set-bit parity |
| `counts` | `counts[0]` values with an even number of ones, `counts[1]` with an odd number |
| `rest` | the bits of `value` not cleared yet |
| `parity` | 1 when an odd number of bits has been cleared so far |
| `countA`, `countB`, `countC` | the parity counts of `a`, `b` and `c` |
| `parityA`, `parityB` | parities picked for the elements from `a` and `b` |
| `total` | triplets counted so far |

narration.2: The helper counts how many values of one array have an even and how many an odd number of 1 bits.
narration.3: counts[0] is for even parity, counts[1] for odd parity.
narration.5: Work on a copy of the value so its bits can be cleared one by one.
narration.6: No bit has been cleared yet, so the parity so far is even.
narration.7: Keep going while some 1 bit is left.
narration.8: rest - 1 flips the lowest 1 bit and the zeros below it, so the AND clears exactly that bit.
narration.9: One more 1 bit: the parity flips.
narration.11: File this value under its parity.
narration.15: Only the set-bit parity of each number matters, so summarise a by its parity counts...
narration.20: Pick the parity of the element from a...
narration.22: The element from c must have parity parityA ^ parityB for an even total; multiply the matching counts.
narration.25: Every combination of parities has been added, which counts all triplets with an even XOR.
